title: Chapter 6.  History — Medieval Kashmir: Sultanate, Mughal, Afghan & Sikh Rule

blocks.content: Kashmir's medieval history sees a major religious and political transformation — the establishment of Muslim rule from the 14th century, followed by successive Mughal, Afghan and Sikh conquests — each leaving a distinct administrative and cultural imprint that remains relevant to the region's identity today.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Shah Mir Dynasty established the Kashmir Sultanate, governing from 1339 to 1586.
Mughal Rule was established in Kashmir in 1586 and lasted until 1752.
The Durrani Empire introduced Afghan Rule over Kashmir from 1752 to 1819.
Sikh Rule governed the region from 1819 to 1846 prior to the treaty establishing Dogra Rule.

blocks.content: Shah Mir, traditionally said to be of Central Asian or Swat-region origin, founded the Shah Mir dynasty and established Muslim rule over Kashmir in 1339, marking the beginning of the Kashmir Sultanate period that lasted, through several successor dynasties, until the Mughal conquest of 1586.

Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (reigned c. 1420-1470), often referred to by the honorific 'Budshah' ('the Great King'), is remembered as Kashmir's most celebrated medieval ruler — noted for religious tolerance toward his Hindu subjects, patronage of arts, crafts (including the introduction/promotion of papier-mache, carpet-weaving, and shawl-making traditions still associated with Kashmir today), and significant public works including irrigation canals and the restoration of temples alongside mosques.

This Sultanate period also saw the gradual, complex process of Islamisation of the Valley's population, significantly shaped by the missionary activity of Sufi saints — most notably Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani ('Shah-e-Hamadan'), a Persian Sufi credited with major influence on Kashmiri Islam, crafts and culture, commemorated today by the Khanqah-e-Moula shrine in Srinagar.

★ EXAM POINT: Zain-ul-Abidin ('Budshah') is Kashmir's most frequently tested medieval Sultanate ruler — remember his reputation for religious tolerance and patronage of Kashmiri handicraft traditions (papier-mache, shawls, carpets) that remain economically significant today (see Chapter 18).
History — Medieval Kashmir: Sultanate, Mughal, Afghan & Sikh Rule

Emperor Akbar annexed Kashmir into the Mughal Empire in 1586, ending the independent Sultanate period; Kashmir subsequently became a favoured summer retreat for successive Mughal emperors, celebrated in Mughal court literature and art for its scenic beauty.

Jahangir and Shah Jahan in particular developed the famous Mughal Gardens of Kashmir — including Shalimar Bagh, Nishat Bagh, and Chashme Shahi in Srinagar — as terraced pleasure gardens along the shores of Dal Lake, which remain among Kashmir's most visited heritage/tourism sites today (see Chapter 24).

Jahangir is famously (though perhaps apocryphally) associated with the phrase describing Kashmir as being akin to paradise on earth — a sentiment that entered popular Persian/Urdu literary tradition and remains closely associated with Kashmir's cultural image.

rows: Foundational period of independent Islamic rule in Kashmir
Integration of Kashmir into the imperial administration of the Mughals
Rule under the Durrani Empire following Mughal collapse
Expansion of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's empire into Kashmir

blocks.content: Following the decline of Mughal central authority, the Durrani Afghan Empire under Ahmad Shah Durrani annexed Kashmir in 1752, beginning a period of Afghan governorship widely remembered in Kashmiri historical memory as harsh and oppressive, marked by heavy taxation and periodic instability under a rotating series of Afghan-appointed governors.
This period of Afghan rule ended in 1819 when the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh conquered Kashmir, incorporating it into the wider Sikh Empire based at Lahore.

Under Sikh administration (1819-1846), Kashmir was governed as a province of Ranjit Singh's Lahore-based Sikh Empire through a series of appointed governors, a period that set the stage for the region's subsequent transfer to Dogra rule following the First Anglo-Sikh War.

items: Memorize the chronological order of rulers in medieval Kashmir: Sultanate -> Mughal -> Afghan -> Sikh.
Pay attention to transition years: 1586 (Mughal annexation), 1752 (Afghan conquest), and 1819 (Sikh capture).
Questions often test the exact period duration for Afghan rule (1752-1819) versus Sikh rule (1819-1846).

blocks.content: This 27-year Sikh interlude is the direct historical bridge to the pivotal 1846 Treaty of Amritsar (covered in full in Chapter 7), which created the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under the Dogra dynasty — the polity whose 1947 accession to India (Chapter 8) and subsequent special constitutional status (Chapters 9-10) form the core of this UT's modern political identity.

★ EXAM POINT: Sequence to remember: Shah Mir Sultanate (1339-1586) -> Mughal (1586-1752) -> Afghan/Durrani (1752-1819) -> Sikh (1819-1846) -> Dogra princely state (1846-1947) -> accession to India (1947) -> present-day UT (since 2019). This full ruling-power sequence is one of the highest-yield timeline questions for J&K history.

items: Shah Mir founded the Kashmir Sultanate in 1339; Sultanate lasted until the 1586 Mughal conquest.
Zain-ul-Abidin ('Budshah', r. c.1420-1470) = most celebrated Sultanate ruler; patron of Kashmiri crafts (shawls, papier-mache, carpets) and religious tolerance.
Akbar annexed Kashmir into the Mughal Empire in 1586; Jahangir & Shah Jahan developed the Mughal Gardens (Shalimar Bagh, Nishat Bagh, Chashme Shahi).
Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan Empire ruled Kashmir 1752-1819, widely remembered as an oppressive period.
Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh ruled Kashmir 1819-1846, ending with the Treaty of Amritsar and transfer to Dogra rule.
